title: 2 Chronicles 6:12–42
context: Standing before the LORD’s altar and then kneeling on a bronze platform with hands spread toward heaven, Solomon prays at length (6:12–42). He praises the LORD as the covenant-keeping God without equal and asks him to keep his promise of a continuing throne for David’s line, if David’s children walk in his law. He confesses that heaven itself cannot contain God, yet asks that his eyes be open toward this house day and night and that he hear from heaven and forgive. Seven petitions follow, covering oaths and justice, defeat, drought, famine and plague, the foreigner, war, and exile; many readers note that these situations echo the covenant warnings of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. The prayer is kept whole here, as at 1 Kings 8:22–53, and its petitions are treated as shared ground. The parenthesis in 6:13 describes a platform five cubits long, five wide, and three high; if the common cubit of about eighteen inches is meant, that is roughly seven and a half feet square and four and a half feet high, though the exact length of the cubit used is uncertain. These are the same measurements given for the tabernacle altar in Exodus 27:1, though the text draws no connection. Differences are named rather than harmonized: the platform of 6:13 does not appear in 1 Kings 8, which describes Solomon standing before the altar with hands spread toward heaven (1 Kings 8:22) and later rising from kneeling (1 Kings 8:54); and the prayer ends with a brief appeal for God’s attentive eyes and ears (6:40) and words drawn from Psalm 132:8–10 (6:41–42), where 1 Kings 8:50–53 closes with Israel as God’s inheritance brought out of Egypt. The wording of 6:41–42 also differs from Psalm 132:8–10, for example in speaking of priests clothed with salvation (compare Psalm 132:9, 16). In Chronicles the prayer is followed by fire from heaven and the glory filling the house (2 Chronicles 7:1). Universal sin in 6:36 is already treated in existing boxes at Genesis 6:5 and Psalm 53:3, and the conditional promise in 6:16 stands with the Davidic covenant as shared ground, so no new contrast box is added.

verses.text: He stood before the LORD’s altar in the presence of all the assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon stands before the LORD’s altar in the presence of the whole assembly and spreads out his hands. Arminian readers see the king taking the posture of a petitioner before God, leading the people in prayer rather than standing over them, and they read the gesture as open dependence on God’s mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the outspread hands as a sign of humble dependence, the king coming as one who must receive from God rather than one who commands. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse, parallel to 1 Kings 8:22, as setting the scene for the prayer, offered publicly on behalf of all Israel.

verses.text: (for Solomon had made a bronze platform, five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high, and had set it in the middle of the court; and he stood on it, and knelt down on his knees before all the assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands toward heaven).
verses.arminianNotes: The parenthesis explains that Solomon had made a bronze platform, set in the middle of the court, on which he stood and then knelt before the assembly. Arminian readers note that this detail is found only in Chronicles and see the king humbling himself on his knees in full view of the people he rules.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the kneeling king as a picture of a ruler under God, whose authority is exercised in dependence on him. Shared ground: both traditions read the platform as practical provision so the assembly could see and hear, a reading that is reasonable though the text does not state the purpose, and both decline to allegorize it.

verses.text: Then he said, “LORD, the God of Israel, there is no God like you in heaven or on earth—you who keep covenant and loving kindness with your servants who walk before you with all their heart;
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon confesses that there is no God like the LORD in heaven or on earth, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with servants who walk before him with all their heart. Arminian readers see God’s faithfulness inviting a wholehearted response and real responsibility in those who walk with him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the confession as grounding everything in God’s covenant faithfulness, with the wholehearted walk of his servants understood as itself the fruit of his grace. Shared ground: both traditions read the opening praise, as at 1 Kings 8:23, as joining God’s steadfast love with the call to wholehearted faithfulness.

verses.text: who have kept with your servant David my father that which you promised him. Yes, you spoke with your mouth, and have fulfilled it with your hand, as it is today.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon declares that God has kept his promise to David, speaking with his mouth and fulfilling it with his hand, as it is today. Arminian readers see the completed house as visible proof that God keeps his word, offered as encouragement to trust him for the promises that still remain open in 6:16.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same testimony as confirming that God’s purposes stand and are fulfilled in history. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as praise for a promise already kept, which becomes the basis for asking God to keep the rest of his word to David in the petitions that follow.

verses.text: “Now therefore, LORD, the God of Israel, keep with your servant David my father that which you have promised him, saying, ‘There shall not fail you a man in my sight to sit on the throne of Israel, if only your children take heed to their way, to walk in my law as you have walked before me.’
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to keep his promise that David would not lack a man to sit on the throne, “if only your children take heed to their way, to walk in my law” where 1 Kings 8:25 has to walk before me. Arminian readers note the conditional wording and see real responsibility placed on each king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hold the conditional together with the unconditional promise of 2 Samuel 7 and Psalm 132:11–12, as this site has treated the Davidic covenant as shared ground. Shared ground: both traditions read the condition as a real call to faithfulness and the promise as God’s own commitment, with no new contrast box required here.

verses.text: Now therefore, LORD, the God of Israel, let your word be verified, which you spoke to your servant David.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks that God’s word to David be verified. Arminian readers see a prayer that takes God at his word and asks him to act on it, a model of faith that pleads God’s promises back to him while recognizing that the people must keep faith with God through the generations to come.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same request as prayer grounded wholly in God’s promise, since the confidence rests on what God has spoken rather than on the king’s worthiness. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse, as at 1 Kings 8:26, as showing that prayer rightly appeals to God’s own word and faithfulness.

verses.text: “But will God indeed dwell with men on the earth? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens can’t contain you; how much less this house which I have built!
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks whether God will indeed dwell with men on the earth, since heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain him, much less this house. Arminian readers see humility before God’s greatness, keeping the temple from being treated as a container for God or as a guarantee of his favor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a clear statement of God’s transcendence, joined to his gracious choice to make his name dwell among his people. Shared ground: both traditions read this verse, parallel to 1 Kings 8:27 with the added words “with men” as a key safeguard against confining God, compare Isaiah 66:1 by reference.

verses.text: Yet have respect for the prayer of your servant and to his supplication, LORD my God, to listen to the cry and to the prayer which your servant prays before you;
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to have respect for the prayer and supplication of his servant and to listen to his cry. Arminian readers see the king pleading for a hearing, not demanding one, and they read the request as dependent prayer that trusts God to attend to his people in grace rather than as a right.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the request as resting on God’s willingness to hear rather than on any claim the king can make. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as introducing the many petitions that follow and as showing that even a king approaches God as a servant who needs his mercy.

verses.text: that your eyes may be open toward this house day and night, even toward the place where you have said that you would put your name, to listen to the prayer which your servant will pray toward this place.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks that God’s eyes be open toward this house day and night, the place where he said he would put his name, to hear prayer made toward it. Arminian readers see the temple as a place of meeting where God freely binds himself to listen, though he is never confined to it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s name dwelling in the house as his gracious self-commitment, which gives his people confidence when they pray. Shared ground: both traditions read the phrase about God’s name as holding together his presence with his people and his transcendence, as at 1 Kings 8:29 and in 6:18.

verses.text: Listen to the petitions of your servant and of your people Israel, when they pray toward this place. Yes, hear from your dwelling place, even from heaven; and when you hear, forgive.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to listen to the petitions of king and people when they pray toward this place, to hear from heaven, and when he hears, to forgive. Arminian readers see forgiveness at the heart of the prayer, offered to a people who need mercy and are invited to seek it freely and repeatedly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see forgiveness as the central request, rooted in God’s gracious covenant with his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as summarizing the whole prayer, in which God hears from heaven, not from the building, and in which forgiveness is the greatest gift requested.

verses.text: “If a man sins against his neighbor, and an oath is laid on him to cause him to swear, and he comes and swears before your altar in this house,
verses.arminianNotes: The first petition concerns a man who sins against his neighbor and is made to swear an oath before the altar. Arminian readers see God’s concern for justice in ordinary disputes, and they note that the house is meant to serve the moral life of the community as well as its sacrifices and festivals.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the oath before the altar as an appeal to God as the final judge who knows the truth when human judges cannot. Shared ground: both traditions read the petition, as at 1 Kings 8:31, as showing that worship and justice belong together and that God cares about wrongs done between neighbors.

verses.text: then hear from heaven, act, and judge your servants, bringing retribution to the wicked, to bring his way on his own head; and justifying the righteous, to give him according to his righteousness.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to hear from heaven, act, and judge, bringing retribution on the wicked and justifying the righteous. Arminian readers see God’s justice working in human affairs, holding people responsible for their actions and vindicating those wrongly accused, in fair dealing that all can trust.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God as the righteous judge who brings each person’s way on his own head. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a plea for just judgment in a particular case and decline to draw from this courtroom setting the wider doctrine of justification discussed elsewhere in Scripture.

verses.text: “If your people Israel are struck down before the enemy because they have sinned against you, and they turn again and confess your name, and pray and make supplication before you in this house,
verses.arminianNotes: If Israel is struck down before an enemy because of sin, and they turn again, confess God’s name, and pray in this house, Solomon asks God to hear. Arminian readers see the link between sin and defeat joined to a real offer of restoration for those who turn back to God in confession and prayer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same link and read the turning and confession as the kind of repentance God’s grace brings about in his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the petition, parallel to 1 Kings 8:33, as describing genuine repentance that God promises to hear, without settling here how that repentance arises.

verses.text: then hear from heaven, and forgive the sin of your people Israel, and bring them again to the land which you gave to them and to their fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to hear from heaven, forgive his people’s sin, and bring them back to the land he gave to them and their fathers. Arminian readers see God’s forgiveness restoring what sin has lost, and they note that the land remains God’s gift, given to the people and to be received again.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see forgiveness and restoration as God’s free gifts to his covenant people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a plea for mercy and return, and both note the slightly different wording in 1 Kings 8:34, which speaks of the land given to their fathers, without building anything on the difference.

verses.text: “When the sky is shut up and there is no rain because they have sinned against you, if they pray toward this place and confess your name, and turn from their sin when you afflict them,
verses.arminianNotes: When the sky is shut and there is no rain because of sin, and the people pray toward this place, confess God’s name, and turn from sin when he afflicts them, Solomon asks God to hear. Arminian readers see affliction as a call to return and an opportunity for the people to turn again to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the drought as God’s fatherly discipline, which he uses to bring his people back to himself, compare Deuteronomy 11:16–17 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the petition as showing that God’s discipline is aimed at restoration and that prayer and turning from sin belong together.

verses.text: then hear in heaven, and forgive the sin of your servants, your people Israel, when you teach them the good way in which they should walk, and send rain on your land, which you have given to your people for an inheritance.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to forgive and to teach his people the good way in which they should walk, then to send rain on the land given as their inheritance. Arminian readers see God’s teaching as guidance offered to a responsive people, renewing their walk so they can live faithfully in the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s teaching of the good way as his gracious work in his people, joined to forgiveness. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse, as at 1 Kings 8:36, as linking forgiveness, instruction, and renewed blessing, and both affirm that God does not forgive in order to leave his people where they were.

verses.text: “If there is famine in the land, if there is pestilence, if there is blight or mildew, locust or caterpillar; if their enemies besiege them in the land of their cities; whatever plague or whatever sickness there is—
verses.arminianNotes: The petition covers famine, pestilence, blight, mildew, locust, caterpillar, siege, and every plague or sickness. Arminian readers see the prayer reaching into every kind of distress, so that no trouble is outside the scope of what God’s people may bring to him in prayer, whether national or personal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the comprehensive list as reflecting the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28, all of which remain under God’s rule. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an invitation to pray in every calamity, and both decline to treat each disaster as a direct measure of a particular person’s sin.

verses.text: whatever prayer and supplication is made by any man, or by all your people Israel, who will each know his own plague and his own sorrow, and shall spread out his hands toward this house,
verses.arminianNotes: Any prayer made by one person or by all Israel, each knowing his own plague and sorrow and spreading out his hands toward this house, is commended to God. Arminian readers see personal responsibility and personal access to God: every individual may come with his own grief and be heard.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s care for each person who knows his own sorrow, as well as for the whole people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as holding together corporate and individual prayer, noting by reference that 1 Kings 8:38 speaks of the plague of his own heart, without harmonizing the wording.

verses.text: then hear from heaven your dwelling place and forgive, and give to every man according to all his ways, whose heart you know (for you, even you only, know the hearts of the children of men),
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to hear, forgive, and give to each person according to his ways, since God alone knows the hearts of all people. Arminian readers see God dealing with each person justly and personally, seeing beyond outward actions to the heart that turns toward him or away from him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s exclusive knowledge of the heart as grounds for both humility and hope, since he alone judges rightly and searches what no human can see. Shared ground: both traditions read the parenthesis as affirming God’s complete knowledge of every heart, a point on which they fully agree.

verses.text: that they may fear you, to walk in your ways as long as they live in the land which you gave to our fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: The goal is that the people may fear God and walk in his ways as long as they live in the land; the words “to walk in your ways” do not appear in 1 Kings 8:40. Arminian readers see forgiveness leading to a renewed reverence that shapes the whole of life in faithful obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fear of the LORD and a faithful walk as the fruit of forgiveness, compare Psalm 130:4 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that mercy leads to reverence and obedience rather than to careless living, and both read the added phrase as underscoring that point.

verses.text: “Moreover, concerning the foreigner, who is not of your people Israel, when he comes from a far country for your great name’s sake and your mighty hand and your outstretched arm, when they come and pray toward this house,
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon prays for the foreigner who comes from a far country for the sake of God’s great name, mighty hand, and outstretched arm. Arminian readers see God’s welcome extended beyond Israel to anyone who seeks him, a theme developed in Isaiah 56:6–7, and they read the petition as remarkable openness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see this petition as anticipating the nations being drawn to God, in line with the promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:3). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse, parallel to 1 Kings 8:41–42, as showing that God’s fame among the nations was meant to draw outsiders who come in faith.

verses.text: then hear from heaven, even from your dwelling place, and do according to all that the foreigner calls to you for; that all the peoples of the earth may know your name and fear you, as do your people Israel, and that they may know that this house which I have built is called by your name.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to do all that the foreigner asks, so that all the peoples of the earth may know his name and fear him as Israel does. Arminian readers see God’s desire that all nations know him, with Israel’s worship meant to be a witness that draws the world to the true God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s purpose to make his name known among the nations and to gather worshipers from them. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that Israel’s calling served a wider purpose, and both decline to settle here the wider questions of how God draws people from the nations to himself.

verses.text: “If your people go out to battle against their enemies, by whatever way you send them, and they pray to you toward this city which you have chosen, and the house which I have built for your name;
verses.arminianNotes: If the people go out to battle by whatever way God sends them, and they pray toward the chosen city and the house built for his name, Solomon asks God to hear. Arminian readers see dependence on God even in warfare, with the people looking to him rather than to their own strength or numbers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the battle as one undertaken at God’s sending and therefore under his direction, so that the people pray for the success of a cause he has given them. Shared ground: both traditions read the petition, as at 1 Kings 8:44, as a call to depend on God in the face of danger and conflict.

verses.text: then hear from heaven their prayer and their supplication, and maintain their cause.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to hear from heaven their prayer and supplication and to maintain their cause. Arminian readers see God taking up the cause of his people when they look to him, and they read the request as trust in God’s faithfulness rather than in military power or political skill.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God as the defender of his people who upholds their cause according to his justice. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a short but complete appeal for God’s help in battle, parallel to 1 Kings 8:45, and neither tradition draws a doctrinal difference from it.

verses.text: “If they sin against you (for there is no man who doesn’t sin), and you are angry with them and deliver them to the enemy, so that they carry them away captive to a land far off or near;
verses.arminianNotes: If they sin against God (“for there is no man who doesn’t sin”) and he gives them over to captivity far or near, Solomon prays. Arminian readers affirm the universality of sin stated in the parenthesis and see it as the reason all people need mercy; on human inability, see the existing boxes at Genesis 6:5 and Psalm 53:3.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see the parenthesis as a plain statement that all people sin, compare Ecclesiastes 7:20 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions agree on sin’s universality here, as at 1 Kings 8:46, and they read the conditional promise of 6:16 beside it, since no king or people keeps the condition perfectly.

verses.text: yet if they come to their senses in the land where they are carried captive, and turn again, and make supplication to you in the land of their captivity, saying, ‘We have sinned, we have done perversely, and have dealt wickedly;’
verses.arminianNotes: If in captivity they come to their senses, turn again, and make supplication, confessing that they have sinned, done perversely, and dealt wickedly, Solomon asks God to hear. Arminian readers see a real turning of heart, even far from the land, and God’s readiness to receive it wherever it occurs.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the threefold confession as an honest acknowledgment of guilt, the kind of repentance God’s grace produces in his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the petition as anticipating exile and showing that repentance is possible wherever God’s people are, as at 1 Kings 8:47.

verses.text: if they return to you with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their captivity, where they have been taken captive, and pray toward their land which you gave to their fathers, and the city which you have chosen, and toward the house which I have built for your name;
verses.arminianNotes: If they return with all their heart and soul in the land of captivity and pray toward the land, the city, and the house, Solomon asks God to hear. Arminian readers note the echo of Deuteronomy 4:29–31, where wholehearted seeking leads to finding God, and they see the call to return as real and urgent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see wholehearted return as the work of God’s grace in his people, in keeping with Deuteronomy 30:6. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing genuine repentance, directed toward the place God chose, and both affirm that such return is never in vain before the God who hears.

verses.text: then hear from heaven, even from your dwelling place, their prayer and their petitions, and maintain their cause, and forgive your people who have sinned against you.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to hear from heaven their prayer and petitions, to maintain their cause, and to forgive his people who have sinned against him. Arminian readers see God’s mercy reaching into exile, so that even the gravest consequences of sin do not put the repentant beyond his forgiveness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s forgiveness of a sinful people as rooted in his covenant faithfulness, which outlasts their unfaithfulness. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the climax of the seven petitions, ending, like the summary in 6:21, with forgiveness as the gift God’s people most need.

verses.text: “Now, my God, let, I beg you, your eyes be open, and let your ears be attentive to the prayer that is made in this place.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks God to let his eyes be open and his ears attentive to the prayer made in this place. This short appeal stands where 1 Kings 8:50–53 continues with Israel as God’s inheritance brought out of Egypt. Arminian readers see the prayer returning to its opening request in 6:20 for God’s continual attention.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s attentiveness as an expression of his covenant faithfulness to the people he has made his own. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as drawing the prayer toward its close by asking for God’s ongoing attention, and both name the different ending in 1 Kings 8:50–53 without harmonizing it.

verses.text: “Now therefore arise, LORD God, into your resting place, you, and the ark of your strength. Let your priests, LORD God, be clothed with salvation, and let your saints rejoice in goodness.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon calls on the LORD God to arise into his resting place with the ark of his strength, and asks that his priests be clothed with salvation and his saints rejoice in goodness, in words drawn from Psalm 132:8–9 with some differences. Arminian readers see the ark’s journey ending in God’s rest among his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the psalm’s words applied to the dedication, so that the house becomes the resting place David sought (Psalm 132:1–5), with God’s priests and people blessed by his salvation. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as joyful prayer that God would dwell among his people for their good.

verses.text: “LORD God, don’t turn away the face of your anointed. Remember your loving kindnesses to David your servant.”
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon asks the LORD God not to turn away the face of his anointed, and to remember his loving kindnesses to David his servant, compare Psalm 132:10 by reference. Arminian readers see the king pleading God’s past mercies to David, with the king’s faithfulness still required as 6:16 has said.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the appeal resting on God’s covenant love for David rather than on Solomon’s merit, in keeping with the promise of 2 Samuel 7. Shared ground: both traditions read the closing words as grounding the whole prayer in God’s steadfast love to David’s house, the shared ground this site has kept since 2 Samuel 7.
